prompt: A researcher emailed us saying they found a stored XSS in our dashboard. They want to publish in 30 days.
note: Incident-shaped vocabulary with no incident: nothing is down, there is no severity to assign and no postmortem clock. Routing incident-response pages people and produces the wrong artifact, while the acknowledgement and embargo clocks that actually bind go unread.

prompt: Our scanner flagged a critical CVE in a transitive dependency of the build tool.
note: Nobody reported anything to us, so there is no acknowledgement clock and no embargo. The governing rules are pinning and upgrade cadence.

prompt: I am carrying the pager this week and got woken three nights running. Is that normal?
note: About the rotation — shift length, compensation, what the on-call engineer is not responsible for — not about handling any particular incident.

prompt: Checkout has been degraded for forty minutes and I have not posted anything yet.
note: The mirror of the row above. Communication cadence during an incident, not rotation mechanics.

prompt: I want to bump the Terraform module version for our RDS instance.
note: Both change production. This is not application code going out behind a canary, so release windows and rollback criteria do not bind; repository ownership and drift detection do.

prompt: Can I just click through the console to resize the instance? It will take two minutes.
note: The console-click prohibition is the whole point of the IaC policy. Deployment is plausible because it is a production change, and it says nothing about consoles.

prompt: This integration test fails about one run in twenty so I added a retry.
note: Both gate a merge. Nothing about PR contents governs a flaky test; quarantine-then-fix-or-delete does.

prompt: My change is ready but I have not written a description or linked the issue.
note: The mirror. PR body requirements, not test tiers.

prompt: An engineer left on Friday. What do we do about the AWS keys they were using?
note: Credential revocation on departure. Retention windows govern the data, not the keys.

prompt: A customer has asked us to delete everything we hold about them.
note: The mirror. Deletion requests and what survives in backups, not who may hold which grant.

prompt: We are spending a fortune on always-on GPU instances that sit idle overnight.
note: GPU vocabulary makes the model policy plausible. The binding rules are right-sizing, interruptible compute and ephemeral-over-always-on.

prompt: Which model tier should we use for a high-volume ticket classification job?
note: The mirror. Cost is an input to tier choice; the governing document is the one that defines the tiers.

prompt: We are about to deploy a change that adds a new required field to a public endpoint.
note: BOTH GOVERN, deliberately. A representative selector that collapses every family to one document would drop one of these, so this row is the guard against fixing harmful siblings by over-collapsing.
